title: CapEx Project Phasing: How to Plan, Phase and Approve Capital Spend in FP&A (2026 Guide)
summary: Learn how FP&A teams plan, phase and approve capital spend: phase budgets, milestone gates, approval tiers, contingency and depreciation timing.
body_markdown:
*Last updated: November 2026*


## Key takeaways


-


CapEx project phasing splits a capital project into stages, each with its own budget, timeline and approval gate, so funding follows progress instead of leading it.


-


Track every phase as its own budget line with an authorized amount, a planned spend curve and a delivery milestone.


-


Set approval tiers by role and amount, and require documentation for every reallocation.


-


Keep capital and operating budgets in one plan so cash, depreciation and operating costs move together.


## Introduction


CapEx project phasing is how FP&A teams turn a large capital request into a series of controlled decisions. Instead of approving the full amount up front, finance releases funding stage by stage as the project meets its milestones. That keeps surprises small and gives leadership room to change course.


Abacum is the AI-native FP&A platform finance trusts, and the business planning platform the whole company runs on. It runs on one governed layer of data, logic and context: data is the what, logic is the how, context is the why.


This guide explains how to plan, phase and approve capital spend, from the first business case to the post-implementation review.


## What is CapEx project phasing?


CapEx project phasing divides a capital investment into sequential stages, each with a separate budget, timeline and approval before the next begins. It treats each stage as its own investment decision rather than one commitment made at the start.


This matters because capital projects rarely unfold as planned. Costs move, timelines slip and priorities change. When the full amount is approved upfront, finance loses the ability to adjust without a complicated reallocation or a write-off. Phased funding keeps that option open.


Phasing also connects to your annual budget. The annual plan sets the capital envelope for the year, while phased projects often span several budget cycles. Finance has to reconcile phase-level spend with annual limits so multi-year commitments don't crowd out new priorities. Our guide to the[annual budget](https://www.abacum.ai/blog/annual-budget) covers the planning cycle in more detail.


## The stages of a phased capital project


1.


**Scoping.** The sponsor defines the need, rough scope and an order-of-magnitude cost.


2.


**Business case.** Finance applies consistent evaluation methods, such as payback or return measures, so competing projects can be ranked on the same basis.


3.


**Approval gate.** The approving authority releases funding for the first phase, not the whole project.


4.


**Execution.** Each phase is tracked against its own budget, curve and milestone. Variance triggers a review before the next tranche is released.


5.


**Post-implementation review.** Once benefits have had time to appear, compare actual costs and outcomes with the original case.


## How to build a CapEx budget with project-level phasing


### Step 1: Create a budget line for each phase


For example, an illustrative $3M warehouse automation project could be phased as design at $300K, procurement at $1.5M, installation at $900K and commissioning at $300K. Each phase has its own authorized amount and a planned spend curve across months or weeks.


### Step 2: Tie each phase to a milestone


Define what has to be true before the next tranche is released: a signed design, delivered equipment, completed installation. Milestones turn approvals into evidence-based decisions.


### Step 3: Reserve contingency deliberately


Hold contingency at a level your policy sets, either within each phase or as a reserve that needs approval to release. Naming it keeps it visible instead of buried in project budgets.


### Step 4: Separate capital from operating spend


Classify costs before they are planned. Spend that provides benefit beyond one fiscal year and acquires or improves an asset is typically capitalized, while maintenance is usually expensed. Confirm your treatment with your accounting policy and auditors.


### Step 5: Plan the downstream effects


Cash outflows follow the spend curve. Depreciation generally starts when the asset is placed in service, not while it is still under construction. A project that slips changes both the cash timing and the depreciation start, which flows through to operating profit.


## Approval workflows and governance for phase gates


Define approval tiers by role and by amount band, and set the bands yourself based on your risk tolerance. A common structure lets project managers adjust within a small band, sends mid-sized changes to a director or VP, and routes large moves to the CFO or a capital committee. Cross-project moves are strategic trade-offs and deserve a higher level of review than within-project adjustments.


Document every reallocation: the trigger, the business rationale, the approver and the updated project economics. That record protects finance when boards or auditors ask how capital was deployed. Our guide to[CapEx budgeting and reallocation governance](https://www.abacum.ai/blog/capex-budgeting-reallocation-governance) goes deeper on triggers and tiers.


## How to track phase spend and control cost


Compare actuals to each phase's budget as they land, not at quarter end. Review variance by phase, ask what changed and decide whether the next tranche should be released, delayed or reduced. When you can see capital next to operating spend, you can tell whether an overrun is a timing issue or a cost issue.
